subject: Economics
description: Covers Lakdawala, Tendulkar, Rangarajan, Alagh committees, MPI, Headcount ratio and Gini coefficient.

questions.stem: The Lakdawala Committee (1993) on poverty estimation in India recommended that poverty lines should be calculated based on:

options.option_text: Calorie consumption norms updated using state-specific price indices (CPI-AL for rural, CPI-IW for urban)
A uniform mixed recall period (MRP) replacing the uniform recall period (URP)
Multi-dimensional factors including education and health, not just calorie intake
A single national poverty line based solely on the wholesale price index

questions.explanation: LAKDAWALA COMMITTEE (1993): Headed by D.T. Lakdawala. Key recommendations: (1) Retained the calorie norms of 2400 kcal (rural) and 2100 kcal (urban). (2) Recommended STATE-SPECIFIC poverty lines instead of a single national poverty line. (3) Used Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL) for rural areas and CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) for urban areas to update prices. It was the standard methodology until the Tendulkar Committee. PYQ FREQUENCY: UPSC GS-3, State PSCs.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which poverty estimation committee in India moved away from calorie-based norms and included expenditures on health and education to calculate the poverty line?

options.option_text: Tendulkar Committee (2009)
Alagh Committee (1979)
Lakdawala Committee (1993)
Dandekar and Rath Committee (1971)

questions.explanation: TENDULKAR COMMITTEE (2009): Headed by Suresh Tendulkar. Major shift in methodology: (1) Abandoned the calorie-based estimation. (2) Included private expenditure on HEALTH and EDUCATION in the poverty line basket (previously assumed to be provided by the state). (3) Adopted Mixed Reference Period (MRP) instead of URP. (4) Resulted in a significantly higher poverty rate estimate (21.9% in 2011-12) compared to the Lakdawala methodology. PYQ FREQUENCY: UPSC Prelims, RBI Grade B.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Rangarajan Committee (2014) on poverty measurement reverted to certain older practices and estimated the poverty line for 2011-12 at what daily per capita expenditure?

options.option_text: Rs. 32 for rural and Rs. 47 for urban areas
Rs. 27 for rural and Rs. 33 for urban areas
Rs. 50 for rural and Rs. 75 for urban areas
Rs. 20 for rural and Rs. 25 for urban areas

questions.explanation: RANGARAJAN COMMITTEE (2014): Setup to review the Tendulkar methodology, which was criticized for keeping poverty lines too low (Rs 27 rural/Rs 33 urban). Rangarajan reverted to calculating a specific nutritional requirement (calories, proteins, fats) and added non-food expenses. It set the daily per capita poverty line for 2011-12 at Rs. 32 for rural and Rs. 47 for urban areas. This raised the estimated poverty ratio to 29.5%. However, the government never officially adopted the Rangarajan report, continuing to use Tendulkar numbers for official tracking. PYQ FREQUENCY: UPSC GS-3, State PSCs.

questions.stem: The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) is published annually by:

options.option_text: Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and UNDP
World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF)
World Economic Forum (WEF)
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and WHO

questions.explanation: GLOBAL MPI: Developed in 2010 by OPHI and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). It measures acute multidimensional poverty across developing countries. Instead of just income, it uses 3 dimensions: Health, Education, and Standard of Living. These are measured using 10 indicators (Nutrition, Child mortality, Years of schooling, School attendance, Cooking fuel, Sanitation, Drinking water, Electricity, Housing, Assets). In India, NITI Aayog publishes the National MPI based on similar methodology. PYQ FREQUENCY: UPSC Prelims, Current Affairs.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In poverty measurement, what is the "Headcount Ratio"?

options.option_text: The proportion or percentage of the population living below the poverty line
The depth of poverty indicating how far below the poverty line the poor live
The ratio of income of the richest 10% to the poorest 10%
The number of dependents per earning member in a poor household

questions.explanation: HEADCOUNT RATIO (HCR): The most basic and widely used measure of poverty. It is simply the percentage of the population whose income or consumption is below the poverty line. Formula: (Number of poor people / Total population) * 100. LIMITATION: It only tells you HOW MANY people are poor, but ignores the depth of poverty (whether a person is Rs 1 below the line or Rs 100 below). The Poverty Gap Index measures the depth. The Gini Coefficient measures inequality. PYQ FREQUENCY: Basic economics definition.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Gini Coefficient is a widely used statistical measure for:

options.option_text: Income or wealth inequality within a nation
The exact percentage of people below the poverty line
The rate of structural unemployment in an economy
The elasticity of tax revenue with respect to GDP

questions.explanation:
GINI COEFFICIENT: Developed by Italian statistician Corrado Gini. It measures inequality among values of a frequency distribution (usually income or wealth). Values range from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). 
- 0 = Perfect Equality (everyone has exactly the same income).
- 1 = Perfect Inequality (one person has all the wealth, everyone else has zero).
It is derived from the LORENZ CURVE (the ratio of the area between the line of perfect equality and the observed Lorenz curve to the area under the line of perfect equality). PYQ FREQUENCY: Highly repeated in SSC, UPSC, Bank exams.

questions.stem: Which committee in 1979 was the first to define the poverty line in India explicitly in terms of minimum nutritional requirements (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban)?

options.option_text: Alagh Committee
Tendulkar Committee
Lakdawala Committee
Dandekar and Rath Committee

questions.explanation: ALAGH COMMITTEE (1979): Task Force constituted by the Planning Commission under Y.K. Alagh. It was the FIRST to officially define the poverty line in India based on minimum daily calorie requirements: 2400 kcal per person in rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas. Based on 1973-74 prices, this translated to Rs. 49.09 per capita per month for rural and Rs. 56.64 for urban areas. Dandekar and Rath (1971) had earlier suggested a uniform 2250 kcal norm, but Alagh made the rural/urban distinction. PYQ FREQUENCY: UPSC Prelims, State PSCs.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Unlike the Headcount Ratio, the Poverty Gap Index captures which additional dimension of poverty?

options.option_text: The proportion of population living below the poverty threshold nationally
The average depth of poverty, showing how far the poor fall below the line
The degree of inequality in consumption expenditure among the non-poor
The total fiscal cost needed to achieve broad-based inclusive development

questions.explanation: B is correct because the Poverty Gap Index (P₁) measures the average shortfall of the poor from the poverty line expressed as a fraction of that line, capturing the depth of poverty rather than mere incidence. Option A describes the Headcount Ratio (P₀). Option C describes the Gini coefficient, which measures inequality among the general population, not the depth at which the poor fall below the poverty line.

questions.stem: The Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 replaced earlier BPL surveys in India primarily to ensure that welfare targeting:

options.option_text: Calorie-based norms were applied uniformly to all rural and urban areas
Automatic exclusion and inclusion criteria replaced error-prone self-reporting
The Gini coefficient was computed separately for rural and urban households
State-specific poverty lines replaced the uniform national planning norm

questions.explanation: B is correct because SECC 2011 used objective automatic exclusion criteria (e.g., owning a motorised vehicle, having a salaried government employee in the family) and automatic inclusion criteria (e.g., homeless households, manual scavengers) instead of the self-declaration approach used in earlier BPL censuses, which was highly susceptible to errors and leakage. Options A, C, and D describe unrelated poverty measurement concepts.

questions.stem: India's official poverty headcount ratios are computed primarily using consumption data drawn from which source?

options.option_text: Annual Health Survey (AHS) conducted by the Census Commissioner of India
Household Consumer Expenditure Survey (CES) conducted by the NSSO/MoSPI
National Family Health Survey (NFHS) conducted by the Ministry of Health
Consumer Price Index for agricultural labourers published by Labour Bureau

questions.explanation: B is correct because all Indian poverty lines and headcount ratios — from the Alagh Task Force through Lakdawala, Tendulkar, and Rangarajan — are anchored to the NSSO (now MoSPI) Household Consumer Expenditure Survey. NFHS (Option C) provides health and nutrition data used in the Multidimensional Poverty Index, while the CPI for agricultural labourers (Option D) is used for price deflation, not primary consumption basket construction.

questions.stem: As per the Tendulkar Committee methodology adopted by the Planning Commission, the poverty line for rural India in 2011–12 was set at approximately:

options.option_text: ₹447 per capita per month for rural households across India
₹816 per capita per month for rural households across India
₹972 per capita per month for rural households across India
₹1,200 per capita per month for rural households across India

questions.explanation: B is correct: the Tendulkar poverty line updated to 2011–12 prices was ₹816/month per capita for rural areas and ₹1,000/month for urban areas. ₹447 (Option A) approximates the 2004–05 rural line. The most tempting distractor is ₹972 (Option C), which is the Rangarajan Committee's 2011–12 rural line — it was higher and the key distinction is that Rangarajan revised the line upward by using a broader basket.

questions.stem: Amartya Sen's 'capability approach' to poverty differs from income- or consumption-based measures primarily by:

options.option_text: Measuring poverty only through per-capita consumption expenditure at household level
Defining poverty as deprivation of basic capabilities, not merely low income
Setting a universal caloric norm as the sole threshold for poverty identification
Focusing exclusively on relative poverty compared to national median income

questions.explanation: B is correct because Sen's capability approach (elaborated in 'Development as Freedom', 1999) defines poverty as the inability to achieve basic capabilities — such as living a healthy life, being literate, and participating in community life — rather than simply having a low income or consumption level. This framework philosophically underpins the UNDP's Human Development Index and the Global MPI. Option C describes the calorie-norm approach used by the Alagh and Lakdawala committees, which Sen's approach explicitly challenges.

questions.stem: Under the Alkire-Foster dual-cutoff method used in the UNDP's Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, a person is classified as multidimensionally poor if their weighted deprivation score across 10 indicators exceeds:

options.option_text: 20% of the total weighted score across health, education, and living standards
33.3% of the total weighted score across health, education, and living standards
50% of the total weighted score across health, education, and living standards
40% of the total weighted score across health, education, and living standards

questions.explanation: B is correct: the Alkire-Foster method applies a second cutoff (k) of one-third (33.3%). A person is 'MPI poor' only if deprivations in indicators with combined weighted score ≥ 1/3 of the maximum. Persons scoring 20–33.2% are classified as 'vulnerable to poverty,' while those above 50% are 'severely poor.' The most common exam error is selecting 50%, assuming a majority of indicators must be deprived before a person counts as MPI poor.

questions.stem: Which of the following poverty indices violates the 'transfer axiom' (Pigou-Dalton condition), meaning the measure remains unchanged when income is redistributed among the poor?

options.option_text: FGT P₂ index, which assigns squared weights to the income gaps of the poorest poor
Sen Index, which embeds the Gini coefficient of consumption among the poor
FGT P₀ (Headcount Ratio) and P₁ (Poverty Gap Index), both distribution-blind
Watts Index, which uses the logarithm of income gaps below the poverty line

questions.explanation: C is correct: P₀ counts only the number of poor regardless of how deep their poverty is, violating both monotonicity and the transfer axiom. P₁ averages income gaps — redistributing income between two poor persons leaves the total gap unchanged, so P₁ also violates the transfer axiom. P₂ (Option A) satisfies the transfer axiom because squaring gaps gives heavier weight to the poorest. The Sen Index (Option B) incorporates the Gini among the poor and satisfies the axiom, as does the Watts Index (Option D) through its logarithmic formulation.
